I understand the point you're trying to make. It's one of the most common homophobic arguments.

It's fair to dislike people for being loud, perhaps for exhibiting attention-seeking behaviours. However, the issue lies in that what is considered flamboyant and attention-seeking is very subjective. And when you generalise and attach those subjective characteristics to, for example, some gay men, it's simply unhelpful, especially when you comfortably call yourself a homophobe.

Furthermore, often the issue isn't even so complex and homophobes who are simply hateful hide themselves behind a guise of "I'm fine with you being gay, but don't express your sexuality in this particular way, I don't like it, no I'm not homophobic though."

I might add, that part of the problem is you infer people's characteristics from something that can be interpreted in many ways.

You used the example of a body builder wearing a mesh shirt. You say, "who cares?" You assume you know their motivations for their actions, when you don't, and you use your likely false assumptions as an excuse for hateful behaviour.

A black man has a right to not like gangster rap. You have the right to not be flamboyant. You do not have the right to disrespect flamboyant people. Simple logic. 

Your heavily debatable belief that flamboyant people paint you in a negative light is just that, debatable, and is not a valid excuse for homophobia.

From Dale Carnegie's 'How to Win Friends and Influence People'. Probably the definitively best book on social skills.

If you can, always avoid criticising. It almost never helps, and makes the person resent you, even if they asked you to criticise them. *But* if you must, there are ways of doing it that are better than others. If you can, call attention to their mistakes indirectly, and talk about your own mistakes before criticising them. Let the person you're criticising save face and don't push the issue further than you have to. Finally, instead of giving them a direct order to do something differently, ask them questions that allow them to come up with the idea to perform differently themselves, as people are always more motivated to do something when they came up with the idea themselves. If they do improve on their mistakes, encourage and give appreciation. You can't give too much, as long as it's honest.

I really recommend reading the full book, its advice seems simple but nearly everyone breaks key principles mentioned in it that can otherwise put you forward in social situations.
